items.followUp: Define an element and give one example.

rubric.why: Identifies a substance as pure matter with a definite composition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a substance is pure matter with a fixed or definite composition.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of a substance.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example.

modelAnswer: A substance is pure matter that has a fixed composition and definite properties.
Water is an example of a substance.

items.followUp: Write the symbol and valencies of phosphorus.

rubric.why: The correct chemical symbol is required.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the symbol As.
Award 1 mark for giving both valencies, 3 and 5.

modelAnswer: The symbol of arsenic is As.

items.followUp: Write two limitations of Bohr’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Rutherford's model could not explain why orbiting electrons do not lose energy and collapse into the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the model could not explain atomic stability or why electrons do not fall into the nucleus.

rubric.why: The model did not explain the observed discrete line spectra of atoms or the arrangement of electrons.
rubric.description: Failure to explain spectra or electron arrangement
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid limitation concerning line spectra or electron arrangement.

modelAnswer: Rutherford's model could not explain the stability of the atom: orbiting electrons should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus.
It could not explain the discrete line spectra of atoms or the arrangement of electrons around the nucleus.

items.followUp: Explain how nuclear fission can be used to generate electricity.

rubric.why: Power generation begins when U-235 undergoes fission, typically after absorbing a neutron, releasing energy and further neutrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining neutron-induced fission of U-235 or the resulting chain reaction.

rubric.why: The released heat is used to produce steam that drives a turbine connected to a generator.
rubric.description: Conversion of nuclear energy to electrical energy
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the heat-to-steam-to-turbine/generator process.

modelAnswer: U-235 absorbs a neutron and undergoes nuclear fission, releasing a large amount of heat and more neutrons that can sustain a chain reaction.
The heat produces steam, which turns a turbine connected to an electric generator.

items.followUp: State Dobereiner’s Triad law and give another suitable example.

rubric.why: A triad consists of three elements with similar chemical properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a triad as three elements with similar properties.

rubric.why: The atomic mass of the middle element is approximately the arithmetic mean of the other two.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the approximate average-mass rule together with a valid example, such as Li, Na, K (7, 23, 39).

modelAnswer: Dobereiner’s Triads are groups of three elements with similar chemical properties, in which the atomic mass of the middle element is approximately the average of the other two.
For example, in Li, Na and K, the atomic mass of Na (23) is approximately the average of Li (7) and K (39): (7 + 39) / 2 = 23.

items.followUp: State the trend in electron affinity across a period and give a reason.

rubric.why: Electron affinity generally decreases in magnitude down a group (becomes less negative).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the general decrease in electron affinity down a group.

rubric.why: Increasing atomic size and shielding weaken the nucleus's attraction for an added electron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid explanation involving greater atomic size or shielding and weaker attraction.

modelAnswer: Electron affinity generally decreases down a group (becomes less negative).
Down a group, atomic size and shielding increase, so the nucleus attracts an added electron less strongly.

items.followUp: Why do ionic compounds usually have high melting points?

rubric.why: Ionic solids contain oppositely charged ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the oppositely charged ions.

rubric.why: Strong electrostatic attractions hold the ions in a fixed lattice, making the compounds solid at room temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking strong ionic attraction or a lattice to the solid state.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds contain positive and negative ions arranged in a fixed lattice.
Strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions hold the lattice together, so ionic compounds are solids at room temperature.

items.followUp: State the type of covalent bond in nitrogen and chlorine molecules.

rubric.why: Each oxygen atom shares two pairs of electrons in an oxygen molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the O₂ bond as a double covalent bond.

rubric.why: Each hydrogen atom shares one pair of electrons in a hydrogen molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the H₂ bond as a single covalent bond.

modelAnswer: An oxygen molecule (O₂) has a double covalent bond, formed by sharing two pairs of electrons.
A hydrogen molecule (H₂) has a single covalent bond, formed by sharing one pair of electrons.
